THE DESIGN

Local foundations. Clear boundaries.

How ByteQuay connects GitHub review and local agent work without turning the desktop app into a remote execution service.

ON THIS PAGEProductArchitectureWorkflowsTrust & dataDesign principlesRemaining work

01 / PRODUCT

One place for the work around a pull request.

ByteQuay is a macOS desktop app for GitHub pull-request work and local agent tasks. Home, watched repositories, PR details, and the embedded browser provide the surrounding context. Task transcripts, approvals, steering, and queues let the user stay involved as work proceeds.

WorkBench connects changes, explanations, and private review. Issues and Jira attach source context to development tasks. Goals keep objectives and accepted outcomes separate from execution attempts; repository memory carries sourced rules, recipes, and specifications into the work.

This overview describes the established foundation. Detailed feature proposals and implementation checkpoints are not release promises.

02 / ARCHITECTURE

A desktop shell and one local backend.

React and TypeScript render the interface inside Electron. A typed IPC bridge connects the renderer to Electron main, which communicates with the Spring Boot sidecar on localhost. SQLite stores durable application facts.

React UI
↕
Electron main
↕
Local backend
↕
SQLite + task files

Agent adapters run the selected provider in a task-owned worktree. GitHub integrations and optional external services sit at the application boundary.

Six backend modules, with distinct responsibilities.

core
Shared domain values and storage contracts.
agent-spi
Provider contracts, capabilities, and normalized events.
agent-core
Task and turn coordination, approvals, queues, and lifecycle rules.
agent-cli
Codex and Claude adapters and owned-process supervision.
persistence-sqlite
Hibernate entities and durable storage implementations.
app
Application services, GitHub integration, HTTP, and runtime composition.

Dependencies point toward framework-free contracts. The application composes the adapters; provider code does not own the database or the desktop transport.

03 / WORKFLOWS

Read locally. Act deliberately.

Pull-request review

Views read cached data first. Refresh paths fetch GitHub state and update the local snapshot. The user inspects descriptions, patches, checks, and activity, then explicitly comments, approves, or merges.

Agent work

A task receives a separate managed worktree. The selected Codex or Claude adapter executes a turn and maps visible provider activity into a shared transcript. Approvals, steering, and queued requests stay attached to that task.

Provider completion and process cleanup are distinct. ByteQuay verifies the owned runtime has stopped before releasing its worktree claim. Normal clean-worktree removal preserves the generated branch.

Embedded GitHub browsing

Electron owns the native WebContentsView surfaces. The app provides navigation while website sessions remain separate from backend credentials. Browser pages do not gain access to the application's privileged bridge.

04 / TRUST & DATA

Local-first has specific meaning.

  • Local application state. SQLite, runtime history, and task files live under the app's local data boundaries. One backend owns the database.
  • A localhost backend. The sidecar is not a public API service. Electron mediates authenticated access from the desktop interface.
  • Explicit authority for writes. GitHub mutations require a direct user action or an explicitly accepted automation scope. Viewing a diff or starting a discussion is not permission to publish.
  • Separate worktrees. Tasks run in app-managed worktrees. Normal cleanup is non-destructive and retains their generated branches.
  • External network services. GitHub requests and selected model-provider traffic leave the Mac. Local-first does not imply offline model inference.
  • Provider permissions remain meaningful. Native sandboxes and approval policies govern tool execution. Worktree separation alone is not a complete security boundary.

05 / PRINCIPLES

Keep the architecture proportionate.

Use the existing application and agent services. Introduce another module or abstraction only when it solves a real dependency, replacement, or testing problem.

Durable records capture facts needed for coordination and recovery. Disposable execution detail stays with task runtime files. Hibernate owns the current schema while the product is pre-1.0.

High-level design explains responsibilities, data flow, and tradeoffs. Source and tests describe implementation detail; temporary plans and verification logs belong outside the public design narrative.

06 / REMAINING WORK

A foundation still taking shape.

ByteQuay is pre-1.0. Goal conversations, research, courses, and accepted work items exist, while broader discovery, retention, and attention integration remain incomplete. Epic item management and progress are planned; Code & Tests is still being implemented.

The saved-key DeepSeek lane has a narrower capability set and incomplete full live-key verification. Delivery and backports have local and fixture evidence, which does not establish a complete live-provider or live-GitHub journey. Jira live-tenant acceptance also needs separate verification.

Future work extends the current services. Automatic merges, implicit remote issue closure, general tool registries, and broad workflow restart recovery are outside the current boundary.
